description: Zenith is six engineering students from Hochschule Heilbronn, TUM and KID. Before anyone lands on the Moon or Mars, crews test their gear on Earth, but few analog sites have good data. We score Earth locations against lunar and Martian terrain using open NASA and space agency data, then show the best matches on an interactive map. Mission planners get a ranked list of places to test, with the reasons for each rank.
summary: Zenith is a web app for choosing where on Earth to rehearse a Moon or Mars mission. You describe the mission in plain words, and a 3D globe flies to the best match. We scored about 30,000 bare-ground cells on a 0.25-degree grid against seven planned base sites, from the lunar south pole to Jezero Crater. The scoring uses seven conditions: temperature, dryness, terrain, albedo, ice, sunlight and rock type. Each match shows its score, what lines up and what doesn’t, the best time of year to go, sliders for your own conditions, hazards, past research at the site, and what Earth can’t test. We never told the engine where agencies test, yet it ranks known analogs such as the Atacama Desert near the top. 24 of its top sites lie within 300 km of a known analog site, where chance would give about 10. It also finds less-studied places that mission teams could survey and use to test equipment and methods before flight. For outreach, there’s a drilling game with a shared leaderboard.
details:
Team Zenith
Surya Pratama, Tahir Atmaca, Mohamed Elmallah, Immanuel Hamonangan, Kshitij Savanna, Redouane Boulerouah

Describe a Moon or Mars mission in your own words, or pick one of seven permanent-base targets such as the lunar south pole or Jezero Crater. A 3D globe flies to the place on Earth where you’d rehearse it.

How it works
We split Earth into a 0.25-degree grid and kept about 30,000 cells of bare ground. Each cell is scored against every Moon and Mars target on seven conditions: temperature (mean, minimum and day-night swing), dryness (rain and soil moisture), terrain (slope, relief and roughness), surface brightness, ice and permafrost, sunlight, and rock type. Scores are weighted by cell area. Where data is missing we leave the cell out instead of guessing, and ice only counts for targets that have ice.

What you get for each site
You get a match score, plus which conditions line up and which don’t. You also get the best month to go, sliders to try your own conditions, a hazards card for wind, dust, heat and cold, and earlier research done at that site. A plain list shows what Earth can’t give you: low gravity, vacuum and radiation. A ground view puts the Earth site next to its Moon or Mars twin in 3D, and the Earth Jukebox turns a site’s data into sound.

Does it work?
We never told the engine where anyone tests. It still ranked the Atacama Desert near the top for Mars, the same desert soil scientists picked for its Mars-like soil. Across all seven targets, 24 of our top sites sit within 300 km of a known analog site, where random bare ground would give about 10. It also turns up places almost nobody has studied, which mission teams could go and survey.

Why it matters
Agencies rehearse rovers, habitats and procedures on Earth before flight. Zenith lets a team find and compare candidate sites for any mission in minutes, and shows how every score was built. For the public, there’s a drilling game with a shared leaderboard.

Built with
Python for the data pipeline. JavaScript, HTML/CSS, three.js and d3 for the globe and charts. Hosted on Vercel.
